name: hebcal
desc: Perpetual Jewish calendar for the command-line
why: Perpetual Jewish calendar with astronomical calculations for the command line; a niche but genuinely computational tool.

brief.what_it_is: Hebcal is a command-line program that prints the days of the Jewish calendar for a given secular (Gregorian) year, or for a single month or date within it. You can switch on or off the Hebrew date, Jewish holidays, the weekly sedra, the day of the week, and the days of the Omer. It can also add candle-lighting, havdalah, fast times, zmanim, sunrise and sunset, and daily learning schedules such as Daf Yomi. Input is a year, month, day, or YYYY-MM-DD date, plus optional location and timezone; output is plain text, tab-delimited, or ISO dates.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes it as a perpetual Jewish calendar for the command line, meant for generating calendars for PDAs and personal calendars. The README says the original motivation for the algorithms was the Tur Shulchan Aruch.
brief.how_it_works: The key routines were originally translations of Dershowitz and Reingold's Lisp calendar code for GNU Emacs. Candle-lighting times were later rewritten using Derick Rethans's timelib, and the program was ported from C to Go in version 5. Sunset and sunrise come from solar calculations based on a city from a built-in database (hebcal cities), or on latitude, longitude, and timezone you supply with --geo and -z.

commands_seen.context: Prints the holidays in October 1992 C.E. (usage example from the README).
Prints dates in the month of Tishrei in Jewish calendar year 5752.
Per the README, prints just the days of the Omer for the current year.
Prints candle-lighting times for the current year for Oshkosh, Wisconsin, using explicit coordinates and timezone.
Lists the cities in hebcal's database that can be passed to -C.
Prints the version number and default values, a status report on customizations.
Adds two named learning schedules (daily Rambam and 929) to the calendar; the option is repeatable.
Build command from the source repository, after installing Go 1.18+ and GNU make.
Slackware-only install via sbotools, per the README.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install, building from source needs Go 1.18 or higher and GNU make 3.79 or later, then make clean all. The default city ('New York') is set when the program is compiled. Set HEBCAL_CITY to pick a different default city, and HEBCAL_OPTS to prepend options (for example --geo and -z) to every run. Running hebcal info shows the current settings.
brief.standout: It is a small, opinionated, old-school program with a very large option set. It covers many learning cycles (Daf Yomi, Mishna Yomi, 929, Rambam, Psalms, Pirkei Avot and more) and sunrise/sunset zmanim from the command line, and it is explicit about the Julian-to-Gregorian switchover of 1752. Its README is candid that the sun-time routines are approximate.
brief.status: Maintained, with some mixed signals. The GitHub README shows a Go build badge, says version 5 was ported to Go, and the copyright runs through 2026, and development has moved to GitHub. The homepage, however, says only the C implementation is maintained, which seems out of date. I did not see a release date or last commit date, so the exact activity level is unknown.
brief.caveats: Candle-lighting times are described by the author as approximations, and the README says they are guaranteed to be wrong above the arctic or below the antarctic circle. The README says Hebrew dates are valid only before sundown on that secular date. The sunup/sundown routines are called 'not accurate enough' in the Bugs section. The README disclaimer says it 'should not be invested with any sort of halachic authority'. Licensing is GPL. The author asks for a message and suggests a donation, but says payment is not required. The homepage and README disagree on the implementation language (C versus Go). Building requires a Go toolchain as well as make.
quotes: Hebcal is a program which prints out the days in the Jewish calendar for a given secular year.
Hebcal’s candlelighting times are only approximations. If you ever have any doubts about its times, consult your local halachic authority.
It should not be invested with any sort of halachic authority.

judge.reason: It makes the Hebrew lunisolar calendar, its holidays, learning cycles, and solar zmanim explorable from a terminal—a distinctive computational rabbit hole beyond a generic calendar.

entry.title: hebcal
entry.tldr: A command-line Jewish calendar that prints holidays, Hebrew dates, Torah portions, candle-lighting times and daily study cycles for any Gregorian year.
entry.deeper_look:
Hebcal prints the days of the Jewish calendar for a given secular year, month or date. You choose what to show: the Hebrew date, holidays, the weekly sedra, the days of the Omer, and more. Add a location and it can also give candle-lighting, havdalah, fast times, sunrise and sunset. Output is plain text, tab-delimited, or ISO dates, so it is easy to feed into other tools.

The author describes it as a perpetual Jewish calendar for the command line, originally meant for generating calendars for PDAs and personal calendars. The README says the original motivation for the algorithms was the Tur Shulchan Aruch. The key routines began as translations of Dershowitz and Reingold's calendar code for GNU Emacs. Candle-lighting times were later rewritten using Derick Rethans's timelib, and version 5 was ported from C to Go.

The idea underneath is that the Jewish calendar is lunisolar. Months follow the moon, years are kept in step with the sun, and a holiday's date has to be computed rather than looked up. Add the 1752 Julian-to-Gregorian switchover, which the program handles explicitly, and a calendar turns into a small, real calendrical-calculation problem. Reading the output next to the source algorithms is a good way into that world.

It also carries many daily learning cycles, such as Daf Yomi, Mishna Yomi, 929, Rambam and Psalms, so the same tool doubles as a study schedule generator.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the holidays in October 1992, the README's own usage example.
Prints candle-lighting times for the current year at explicit coordinates and timezone (Oshkosh, Wisconsin).
Shows the version number and current default settings, including the default city.

entry.whats_unique: A small, old-school program with a very large option set, covering many learning cycles and sunrise/sunset times from a single command. It is open about where its calculations are approximate.
entry.caveats: The author calls candle-lighting and sunrise/sunset times approximations, guaranteed wrong above the arctic or below the antarctic circle, and says the tool should not be given any halachic authority.
